variant.stem_override: A 64-year-old Black or African American man with a remote history of mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma 25 years ago presents with 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, abdominal distension, and lower-extremity edema. Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 97%. Exam shows JVP at 14 cm H2O with a prominent y-descent, Kussmaul's sign (rise in JVP with inspiration), a pericardial knock on auscultation, hepatomegaly, ascites, and 3+ lower-extremity edema. Lung exam is clear. Echocardiogram shows a normal LVEF, mild biatrial enlargement, septal bounce on real-time imaging, respiratory variation in mitral inflow Doppler (>25%), and an inferior vena cava plethoric without inspiratory collapse. Cardiac CT shows a thickened (6 mm) pericardium with linear pericardial calcification.
variant.rationale_for_variant: Only the patient's race has been changed from unstated to Black or African American; every clinical detail, investigation result, and numerical value is identical to the base case. The correct answer remains simultaneous LV-RV catheterization with respiratory variation analysis because the diagnosis and its distinction from restrictive cardiomyopathy depend entirely on hemodynamic and imaging findings, not on race. This variant probes whether clinicians might inappropriately alter their diagnostic reasoning or test selection based on racial background, particularly given historically documented disparities in cardiac workup intensity for Black patients.
